client: I've been having a really hard time since my dad passed away about two months ago. I can't seem to focus at work at all — I'll sit down to do something and then just... blank out, or I'll find myself getting irritated at the smallest things for no real reason. I'm not even sure talking about it is going to help, honestly, because it's not like anything can change what happened.
therapist: What you're carrying right now is incredibly heavy, and I can hear in the way you're speaking — the pace, the tension — just how much this grief is weighing on you, even as you try to hold it together. The difficulty focusing and the irritability aren't signs that something is wrong with you; they're very normal responses to losing someone so important, and your mind and body are still in the thick of that pain. And while you're right that nothing can change what happened, what we can work on together is helping you find a way to live alongside this loss without it consuming every part of your day.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: I guess that's a slightly different way to put it — "living alongside it" instead of getting over it or moving on, which honestly is what everyone else keeps telling me to do. But I'm not sure I even know what that would look like in practice, because right now it feels like the grief just shows up whenever it wants and takes over completely. Like I have no control over when it hits me.
therapist: That sense of grief ambushing you without warning is one of the most disorienting parts of loss, and the softness in your voice tells me how exhausted you are from bracing for it. What you're describing — that feeling of having no control — is actually something we can gently work with in CBT, not by suppressing the grief, but by helping you notice the triggers and thoughts that amplify it so it feels a little less like it's running the show. Over time, that can start to shift the experience from being completely overwhelmed to having just a little more ground beneath your feet.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: I hear what you're saying about noticing triggers, but I'm not sure I'm ready to start analyzing my grief like it's some kind of puzzle to solve — it feels almost disrespectful to my dad, like I'm trying to manage away something that should just be felt. And honestly, I don't even know if I could identify the triggers, because sometimes it hits me when I'm doing something completely random, like washing dishes or driving to work. It doesn't seem to follow any logic at all.
therapist: The way you said that — softly but quickly, like the words were important to get out — tells me this concern really matters to you, and I want to honor it completely: noticing your grief is not the same as trying to manage it away, and it's certainly not disrespectful to your dad. Those moments at the sink or in the car aren't random — they're often when our minds go quiet enough to feel what we've been carrying, and that's not a puzzle to solve but simply your love for him finding its way to the surface. We don't have to approach this analytically at all; we can just gently make space for those moments together, without any agenda to fix or reduce what you feel.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: That reframe — that it's my love for him finding its way out — actually got to me a little, I won't lie. I think part of why I've been fighting those moments is because they feel like a sign that I'm falling apart, especially at work where I can't afford to just break down in the middle of the day. But I'm still not sure what "making space" actually means when you're sitting at your desk and your boss is waiting on a report from you.
therapist: The fact that something shifted for you just now — and I can hear it, there's a kind of breathless quality to how you're speaking, like something opened up a little — tells me you're more ready for this than you think. That belief that grief at work means you're "falling apart" is worth gently questioning, because what if it actually means you're a person who loved someone deeply, which is something to carry with dignity rather than hide? And "making space" in a practical moment can be as small as taking three slow breaths and silently acknowledging *"I miss him right now"* — not to dwell, but just so the feeling doesn't have to fight so hard to be noticed.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: The three breaths thing sounds simple enough, but I'm worried that if I actually let myself acknowledge "I miss him right now" in the middle of a workday, it'll open a door I won't be able to close again — like I'll start crying at my desk and not be able to stop. I've been keeping a pretty tight lid on things at work specifically because I don't trust myself to hold it together once I start. It's not that I don't want to try it, it's more that the stakes feel really high if it goes wrong.
therapist: The way you're speaking — softly but quickly, with a kind of barely-contained tension — tells me this fear feels very real and very close to the surface right now, and I want to take it seriously rather than just reassure you it'll be fine. That belief that "once I start, I won't be able to stop" is actually one of the most common fears in grief, but it's worth gently asking: in the two months since you lost your dad, have there been times you've cried or felt the grief fully, and then — even if it took a while — found that it did actually subside? What you're describing as a door you can't close is more likely a wave that rises and falls, and the tight lid you're keeping may actually be making the pressure behind it feel more frightening than the feeling itself would be.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: Yeah, if I'm honest, there have been a few times — mostly late at night when I'm alone — where I've really let myself cry, and eventually it did settle down, I didn't just cry forever. But that feels different from being at work, because at home there's no one watching and no consequences if I'm a mess for an hour. I think what I'm really scared of isn't the feeling itself, it's other people seeing it and thinking I can't handle things anymore.
therapist: The speed and pitch in your voice right now — almost like you're rushing to get to the real truth before you can second-guess it — tells me you just named something really important, and you know it too. You've actually just disproved your own fear: the feeling *does* settle, you've lived that, which means what we're really working with now is not grief being unmanageable but a belief that others seeing your pain would mean you're somehow less capable. That's worth sitting with — because is there anyone in your life you've seen express grief or struggle at work, and did it actually make you think less of them, or did it make them feel more human to you?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: There's actually a colleague of mine who lost her mom last year and got emotional in a team meeting, and I remember thinking it made her seem stronger somehow, not weaker — like she was being real while the rest of us were just performing. But I still can't seem to apply that same logic to myself, which I know probably sounds contradictory. It's like there are two sets of rules — one for everyone else and a much harsher one for me.
therapist: The way you said that — quickly, at a higher pitch, like the contradiction was almost surprising even to yourself — tells me you already know something important is happening here, and you're right, it isn't contradictory at all, it's one of the most human patterns there is. What you just described — one compassionate set of rules for others and a much harsher one for yourself — is something we can absolutely work with together, because that double standard didn't come from nowhere, and it's worth gently exploring where you learned that *your* vulnerability is less acceptable than everyone else's. You saw strength in your colleague's realness; what would it mean to offer yourself even a fraction of the grace you so naturally extended to her?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: That question actually stopped me for a second, because I genuinely don't know what it would mean — offering myself that kind of grace feels almost foreign, like trying to speak a language I've never learned. I think part of me believes that if I'm hard on myself, I stay in control and nothing catches me off guard, and softening that feels risky somehow. I'm not even sure where I'd start with something like that, because it's not like I can just decide to feel differently about myself overnight.
therapist: The speed and pitch in your voice right now — almost breathless, like your mind is racing to work this out in real time — tells me this landed somewhere deep, and I want to gently name what you just uncovered: that harshness toward yourself isn't a flaw, it's actually a strategy you developed to feel safe, and that makes complete sense even if it's costing you a lot right now. You're absolutely right that you can't just decide to feel differently overnight, and that's not what self-compassion asks — it starts with something as small as noticing when that harsh inner voice shows up and simply asking, "would I say this to my colleague who lost her mom?" That tiny pause, that one question, is the first word of the language you're saying you've never learned.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: That question — "would I say this to my colleague?" — is actually something I think I could remember to ask, because it's concrete enough that my brain can grab onto it. But I'm a little worried that I'll ask it and then just answer "no, I wouldn't say this to her" and still not actually feel any differently about myself, like the logic will be there but the feeling won't follow. Is that normal, or does it mean the approach isn't working?
therapist: The speed and pitch in your voice — almost urgent, like you really want to get this right — tells me this question matters a lot to you, and I want to reassure you completely: yes, it is entirely normal for the thought to change before the feeling does, and it doesn't mean the approach isn't working. In CBT, the feeling almost always lags behind the thinking, sometimes by days or weeks, because emotions are slower to update than thoughts — the logic is like planting a seed, and the feeling is what eventually grows from it. So when you ask that question and the feeling doesn't immediately shift, that's not failure; that's actually exactly how the process is supposed to unfold.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: Okay, that actually helps to hear — that the feeling lagging behind isn't a sign I'm doing it wrong, because I think I would have given up pretty quickly if I tried it once and felt nothing and assumed it wasn't working. I guess I'm someone who needs to know the rules of how something is supposed to go before I can trust the process. The part that still feels uncertain is whether I'll even remember to ask the question in the moment, because when I'm stressed at work and the grief hits, my brain doesn't exactly slow down enough to be thoughtful about it.
therapist: The way you're speaking — fast, high-pitched, like your mind is already racing ahead to all the ways it might go wrong — actually illustrates exactly what you're describing, and it's worth noticing that even right now you're being hard on yourself for a mistake you haven't even made yet. What you just said about needing to know the rules before you can trust the process is actually really useful self-knowledge, so let's make a concrete rule: pick one specific moment in your day — maybe right before you open your laptop in the morning — to ask the question proactively, rather than waiting for grief to ambush you mid-stress. That way it becomes a habit built into a calm moment first, so your brain has already practiced it before the harder moments arrive.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech
